title: Mental Math & Calculation Shortcuts
shortDescription: The calculation toolkit that sits underneath every other Quant topic — squares, fast multiplication, and percentage-fraction conversions you should recognise on sight.
genZNote: This isn't a new topic, it's your calculator replacement. Learn these ten tricks once, reuse them in literally every question after this one.

sections.heading: Why Start Here
sections.body: Every Quantitative Aptitude topic — Percentage, Profit & Loss, Time & Work, Ratio — eventually comes down to doing arithmetic fast under time pressure. The formulas you'll meet in each topic tell you WHAT to calculate; this page is about HOW to calculate it in your head instead of doing long multiplication on scratch paper. None of this is a substitute for understanding the concept. It's what you reach for once you already know what to compute and just need to compute it fast.

sections.heading: Squaring Numbers Near a Round Base
sections.body: For a number close to a round base (10, 50, 100), square the base and adjust using the difference — this avoids multiplying two two-digit numbers directly.

steps.name: Near 100: (100 ± d)²
steps.purpose: Turns a 3-digit multiplication into two additions.

steps.name: Near 50: (50 ± d)²
steps.purpose: Same idea, smaller base — useful when the number sits between 40 and 60.

steps.name: Near 10: (10 ± d)²
steps.purpose: Fastest for two-digit numbers close to a multiple of 10.

sections.heading: Multiplication by Common Factors
bullets: ×9 → multiply by 10, then subtract the number once. 47 × 9 = 470 − 47 = 423.
×11 (two-digit number) → split the digits and insert their sum in the middle. 45 × 11 → 4_(4+5)_5 = 495. If the middle sum exceeds 9, carry the extra digit left.
×99 → multiply by 100, then subtract the number once. 68 × 99 = 6800 − 68 = 6732.
×101 → multiply by 100, then add the number once. 68 × 101 = 6800 + 68 = 6868.

table.caption: Recognising these on sight turns 'find 33⅓% of 246' into 'find ⅓ of 246' — division by 3, not a percentage calculation at all.

sections.heading: Estimation & Cancelling Before You Multiply
bullets: Cancel common factors between numerator and denominator BEFORE multiplying out — it keeps the numbers small the whole way through instead of building one huge product you then have to simplify.
When an option set is spread far apart (e.g. 420, 1050, 3200, 8000), you often only need the right order of magnitude, not the exact value — round each number to 1–2 significant figures and estimate.
Unit-digit check: for a multiplication or power question, you can eliminate options whose last digit doesn't match the last digit of your calculated result, without finishing the full calculation.

sections.heading: When NOT to Rely on These
sections.body: Every shortcut here assumes exact values matter and the numbers actually fit the pattern (near a round base, a clean fraction, etc.). If the options are close together in value, estimation-based shortcuts can pick the wrong one — switch to the precise method. If a number doesn't sit near 10/50/100, forcing the near-base square trick just adds a slower detour; plain multiplication is faster at that point.

sections.heading: Exam Strategy
bullets: Scan a calculation for a recognisable shortcut (round base, common fraction, ×5/×25/×125) before defaulting to standard multiplication or division.
Practise these until they're automatic — reaching for a trick and then fumbling it costs more time than just doing the direct calculation.
Keep the fraction–percentage table memorised cold; it's reused in nearly every Percentage, Profit & Loss, and Data Interpretation question.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: A toolkit of fast, exact mental-calculation techniques — near-base squaring, common-factor multiplication, and fraction-percentage equivalence — used across every other Quant topic.
keyFacts: (100 ± d)² = 10000 ± 200d + d²; same pattern works for any round base.
×11 on a two-digit number: split digits, insert their sum in the middle, carry if the sum exceeds 9.
1/3 = 33⅓%, 1/8 = 12.5%, 1/6 = 16⅔% — memorise the fraction-percentage table, don't recompute it each time.
commonConfusion: These are calculation shortcuts, not solving methods — they speed up arithmetic you already know you need to do, they don't tell you which formula to apply.

highYieldFacts: The fraction-percentage table (halves, thirds, quarters, fifths, eighths) is reused across nearly every Percentage and Profit & Loss question.
×11 shortcut and ×5/×25/×125 shortcuts save real time on Simplification and Data Interpretation questions with large numbers.
commonTraps: Forcing a near-base square trick on a number that isn't actually close to a round base — check the gap is small (single digit or low double digit) before using it.
Using estimation when the answer options are close together — estimation only works safely when options are well spread apart.
